Registered Office: Charles House, 108-110 Finchley Road, London NW3 5JJ August 2012 Vol 40 No 2 ### The shortage of labour in the Chilean copper mining industry _page 2_ The number of workers employed in Chile’s mining industry has doubled to almost 200,000 during the past decade, with the number employed directly in copper mining surpassing 30,000. The cost of labour in Chile has increased primarily as a consequence of growth in national production. We estimate that demand for workers for the construction of projects could peak to 15,000 in forthcoming years, putting increased pressure on the labour market. 2011 CRU International Limited confidential www.cruonline.crugroup.com
www.cruonline.crugroup.com COPPER STUDIES August 2012 ### Chile’s labour shortage ###### Introduction Labour supply is becoming an increasing challenge for mining operations, not only as workers demand higher wages, but mainly as skilled labourers are becoming increasingly scarce across all regions. There are several indications of tightening labour supply, and the situation is unlikely to reverse in the immediate future. Existing mining operations are forced to operate with a limited labour resource, while mining projects are struggling to populate their operations. In fact, due to the shortage of skilled workers, some new operations are recruiting at the expense of existing operations.

Chile is no exception to this trend, and in this article we analyse the evidence supporting this. Unsurprisingly, workers are taking advantage of the opportunities presented by the undersupply of labour and we are seeing increased mobility at all levels. These labour shortages have equipped workers with increased bargaining power in negotiations with their employers and this has been a contributing factor to a wave of disruptive strikes and demonstrations in Chile that has been observed in recent years. ###### How many are there? CRU estimates that there are currently in excess of 30,000 workers permanently employed by the largest operating copper mines in Chile, which cumulatively account for 90% of the country’s production. In the table overleaf, we can see the distribution of workers at the main mining operations in 2011. Our estimate amounts to around half the number that _Sernageomin_ (National Service of Mining and Geology) considers the total of “principal mining workers” in the country, which we understand refers to directly employed permanent staff. The estimates that _Sernageomin_ provides are understood to be for the entire industry, inclusive of the entire copper supply chain as well as that of other metals and minerals, however, there are no specifications of which companies or types of workers they represent. It is unlikely that copper mining would account for just half of the total workforce of the Chilean mining industry, as copper mining is by far the largest mining sector in the country. We therefore assume that the _Sernageomin_ estimates refer to the total number of workers employed at: small mining operations (which are usually labour intensive); projects in all stages of development (exploration, development, etc.), exploration companies; construction companies, service providers (i.e. engineering firms); and even semi manufactured industries (i.e. processed copper cathode or steel). The chart on Page 4 shows that since 2007, the total number of mining workers in Chile has hit annual records, with the total number of contract workers growing at a proportionately higher rate. As a result, the ratio of directly employed staff to contract workers has increased from 1:1 in 2001 to 1:2.2 in 2011. Hiring contract workers is a flexible alternative to increasing the payroll on a permanent basis. Amongst other Chilean analysts, estimates of the ratio of directly employed staff to contract workers employed at Chilean copper mining companies ranges from 1:1 up to 1:4, which would represent 30,000 to 120,000 contract workers in the sample of mines included in the table below. 2012 CRU International Limited confidential www.cruonline.crugroup.com COPPER STUDIES August 2012 3 |Directly emplo|yed workers by|largest Ch|ilean mining

The workers’ benefits depend on their employment agency and not on the mine operator. However, in the past few years, we have seen an increasing number of contract workers claiming benefits and being incorporated as members of the permanent staff following campaigns and protests. Some of these changes were supported by permanent workers. As the ratio of contractors to permanent workers increases, the bargaining power of permanent workers diminishes, as strikes can be undermined using contractors to fill positions. We, therefore, see a motivation for permanent workers to support contractor strikes and to press for more permanent roles. Thus far, mining companies have been very resistant to addressing the contractors’ concerns, stating that the matter is an issue between them and their direct employers. 2012 CRU International Limited confidential www.cruonline.crugroup.com COPPER STUDIES August 2012 4 Number of workers in Chilean mining industry hit new record, with contractors taking the lead Contractor workers /

In 2007, a number of legislative guidelines were introdu

ced in Chile, aimed at improving the working conditions of contract workers. They enabled the principal company (i.e. the mining company) to voluntarily share responsibility for the contract workers’ benefits and to have the right to audit the compliance of the contractor company to its workers’ rights. The contractor companies have the same rights over their subcontractors. However, there is not enough evidence to show how effective the guidelines have been in practice. In fact, as we have seen, the ratio of contract workers to directly employed workers appears to have been increasing over the past decade. Similarly, the number of contractor companies has also been on the rise. According to _Sernageomin_ , the number of mining companies in Chile rose by 9.4% y-o-y in the last decade to almost 4,000 in 2011. Of this total, the principal companies (i.e. the ones that actually own/run operations) accounted for only 15-20% of the total, experiencing much slower growth than contractor companies. 2012 CRU International Limited confidential www.cruonline.crugroup.com COPPER STUDIES August 2012 5 ###### Future labour demand The sheer quantity of imminent copper mining projects is not only putting pressure on labour availability for the operating phase, but also for the construction phase. We understand that the supply of workers for the construction of projects is inadequate to demand from forthcoming project developments in Chile. Based on our calculations, if all the major projects that have confirmed their development plans break ground on schedule, the industry will be over 15,000 workers short for the construction phase (see chart below). However, our calculation assumes that the projects will require the maximum number of workers throughout the entire construction process, which is unlikely. Nevertheless, if we consider that smaller projects and other large projects (i.e. now with high probabilities of development but no confirmation yet) are also in the pipeline, then it seems more likely that demand for construction workers will severely exceed supply. The aforementioned 15,000-worker requirement is equivalent to around half the number of full time employees currently working at the largest copper mines. Looking ahead, we estimate that the projects in our sample may require around 10,000 workers during their operation stage. It is likely that a significant por

tion of this total will be satisfied by workers already in the market, mainly because some of these projects are expansions or extensions of ongoing operations. However, we can only conclude that demand for workers for both construction and operation of copper mines will continue to rise and the labour market is set to remain tight. ###### Tightness in labour market is not isolated to copper mining The above mentioned tightness in the labour market in the mining industry is not isolated from the rest of the Chilean economy. The country’s economy has been performing in such a way that its national unemployment rate has decreased from 10% in 2009 to 7% in May 2012. Meanwhile, real salaries grew by almost 5% between 2009 and 2011, with the cost of labour rising by 11% in the same period. There are economic studies supporting the theory that, in practice, an employment rate of approximately 5% is 2012 CRU International Limited confidential www.cruonline.crugroup.com COPPER STUDIES August 2012 6 the lowest possible, as there will always be a portion of the workforce that is moving between jobs or in some other form of transition that will label them as “temporarily unemployed” at the time of the survey. As a consequence, full employment will deter workers migrating into mining from other domestic industries. According to Q1 2012 data, the total Chilean population stands at 17.4M people, with 78% of them aged 15 years or older. 13.6M of this total are people of working age, with 8.1M in the labour force and 5.5M who are unable to work for various reasons. Just 7% of the 8.1M labour force is thought to be unemployed. Consequently, we see that the almost 200,000 workers that _Sernageomin_ considers employed in the mining industry makes up only around 3% of the employed labour force in Chile. ##### Cost of labour rises alongside production growth in Chile Indexes of Chilean production and cost of labour (INE updated methodology in 2009)

###### Labour unrest linked to labour shortages A problem stemming from the shortage of labour in Chile is that of labour unrest. Over the past few years, Chile has experienced a wave of strikes and demonstrations that have posed an increasingly severe threat to mine production. As mining companies struggle to secure adequate numbers of skilled workers, an increasing portion of bargaining power is transferred from the hands of mining companies to the workforce and their trade unions. As a result, we deem labour shortages to constitute a major factor facilitating labour unrest, albeit not usually its direct trigger. Certainly, the cause of labour unrest in Chile cannot be purely accredited to a shortage of workers, as a number of other factors can play a significant role. This was clearly apparent in 2011, a year which saw one of the highest incidences of strikes at copper mines in Chile, and around the world. The most oftquoted cause behind strikes in Chile during this period was the mine workers’ dissatisfaction with being inadequately rewarded in light of rising copper prices and record company profits. This led many unions to demand wage and bonus increases and improved benefits across numerous Chilean operations. However, we believe that the force that facilitated many of these strikes was in fact the undersupply of labour which significantly empowered workers and their unions in the eyes of their employers. 2012 CRU International Limited confidential www.cruonline.crugroup.com COPPER STUDIES August 2012 7 In some cases, unions felt so powerful that strikes were even organised outside of the contract renegotiation window, most notably, at the Escondida mine during a two-week strike in July/August 2011. Although the unions at Escondida were largely unsuccessful in securing their requests, the incident showcased their newly-found strength, which allowed workers to feel powerful enough to stand up to one of the world’s largest mining companies at the world’s largest copper mine, outside of the traditional renegotiation period. The episode culminated in a production loss of 40,000t of contained copper. Moreover, it seems that the improved bargaining power stemming from mine labour shortages has not been limited to the directly employed permanent workforce. In May/June 2011, 10,000 contract workers at Codelco’s El Teniente mine staged a strike spanning almost three weeks, causing a production loss of 17,100t of contained copper. The contractors demanded better benefits from the mine operator in protest against their remuneration package compared to that of their permanently employed counterparts. This is unique, in that contract workers are paid by their contractor company, not the mine operator. However, the workers’ increased bargaining strength allowed them to directly challenge the mine operator. The strike ended with the contra

ct workers being awarded improved benefits from the contractor company, however, there have been unconfirmed reports that these benefits were in fact indirectly funded by Codelco. Although 2012 has seen few major strikes in Chile, the majority of strikes and strike threats in this period were reportedly orchestrated by contract workers. Overall, Chilean mine operators find themselves in an increasingly vulnerable position in dealing with their workers’ demands. The prevailing labour shortage has ensured that they are less able to threaten strikers with redundancies or undermine strike action with strike-breakers. Furthermore, with many existing mine operators engaged in mine project developments in Chile, they are increasingly forced to appease their workforce, faced with the prospect of losing them to competing operations. The incidence of major strikes in Chile has declined substantially thus far in 2012, with few contracts due for renegotiation. However, as many Chilean mines enter the next major round of contract renegotiations in late 2012 and early 2013, we can expect a resurgence of disruptive strikes supported by an ever-tightening labour market. In particular, the volume of lost production due to strike action and labour-related disruption has been much lower, as discussed in the previous article. Ore grades have been lower in many mines, but at Escondida there has been a big recovery in grades in H1 due to the Escondida Ore Access Project. On the downside, however, there have been a number of incidences in H1 of stakeholders taking action that could disrupt operations or projects and possibly deter investment. We can broadly split stakeholder disruption into two main categories: - Governmental disruption. This typically involves so-called “resource nationalism”, whereby governments aim to increase revenues from operations or insist on domestic raw materials processing. - Local community disruption. This typically flares up over perceptions of risk to the environment, community health and/or

water supplies, leading to protest action from local communities over environmental or social issues In this article we look at recent incidences of governmental and local community disruption and their impact on existing operations and projects. ###### Governmental disruption Examining governmental disruption and resource nationalism first of all, this is a trend which has intensified during the commodities super-cycle. Governments and their electorates have, of course, noticed the boom in metals prices in the last decade, and the perception of the revenues of mining companies often leads to the conclusion that the national or local share of profits is too low. As the chart below indicates, typical major changes to government mining codes or policies involve raising royalties or blocking the export of raw materials (either by an outright ban or via prohibitive taxation). The most recent announcements of mineral tax increases came from the governments of the Philippines, South Africa and the DRC, and this follows increases in major copper mining countries Chile, Peru, Zambia and Poland in the last couple of years. With the development of Oyu Tolgoi well underway, the government of Mongolia has also imposed a steep additional surtax. Typically governments claim that the additional revenue will be used to fund anti-poverty initiatives or social programmes to aid the poorest sectors of society, or to fund infrastructure development or environmental programmes. The increases to royalties introduced in Chile, Peru, Zambia and Poland were discussed in detail in our January report. KGHM’s Q2 financial report highlights the impact of the new tax on the financial position of the company. The company posted second quarter consolidated net profits of zł.1.34B, down by 41% from zł.2.28 billion a year earlier. KGHM expects to pay full-year levy of zł.1.3 billion this year. In the Philippines, the government completed its review of the mining law in June, but a new mining tax has yet to be passed by Congress. Currently a 2% excise duty is paid on net profits, but it is proposed to introduce a royalty of between 5 and 7%. A proposal for a 7% single levy for all mining operations is under consideration by the department of finance. Steps are also being taken to lift the moratorium on new mining applications with an executive order issued by Philippines’ president Benigno Aquino III on July 9th requiring local mining regulation to be consistent with national laws. However, the ban on open pit mining in South Cotabato remains in place and there is still local opposition to the Tampakan project. This project is facing fierce opposition from NGOs, the Catholic Church and local communities, whose lobbying had caused the ban on open pit mining to be created in the first place. These groups are opposed on the grounds of environmental damage with the removal of areas of rainforest, potential pollution and changes to the way of life of locals. The operator, Sagittarius Mines, recently stated that it does not expect to be able to start the construction of the mine before 2014. A new mining code in the DRC is expected to be in place by the end of 2012. As well as introducing an increase in mining taxes, this will require an overhaul of all mining contracts with international companies. The new code will allow the government to scrap tax holidays and concessions granted to mining companies at the end of the civil war in 2003 and there will be a requirement for a minimum of 35% government ownership in new projects. Besides the trend for increasing resource taxes, there is also widespread enthusiasm amongst the governments of the developing world for the idea of bringing downstream processing into their countries to gain further value share and jobs. The prevailing view is that since the mineral resources of a country, once mined, can only be processed and sold once, so it should be done domestically at optimal revenue and benefit to the country. However, the truth of the copper market is that smelting and refining will only provide the last 10% or so of value, and with a global raw materials deficit set to continue beyond the refined deficit (primarily due to continuing Chinese smelter capacity expansions) the world is more in need of copper

concentrate exporting mines than new copper smelters. 2012 CRU International Limited confidential www.cruonline.crugroup.com COPPER STUDIES August 2012 10 The government of Zambia has imposed a ban on raw material exports, while the government of Indonesia has announced that exports will be banned in future and in the meantime a 20% tax has been imposed on exports unless plans are in place to build processing capacity. In the case of copper in Indonesia, both FCX and Newmont are exempt from the tax because together they fully supply the existing smelting capacity in the country, and they are also protected by their existing contracts of work. However they would be obliged to supply any new smelting capacity. The Indonesian mines are major suppliers of concentrates to the Japanese and other Asian smelters as well as Atlantic Copper in Spain. In Zambia, the mining and smelting industry is already heavily integrated and the two large custom mines, Lumwana and Kansanshi also largely supply domestic smelters. First Quantum is also constructing a 300,000t/y smelter at Kansanshi to process concentrates from its Sentinel project and an expansion at the Kansanshi mine. ###### Local community disruption Local community disruptions have much broader motivations. They may also be motivated by money or enhancements to local services (schools, hospitals etc), but just as frequently, if not more so, their main concern is preserving their current quality of life. Apprehensions tend to centre on access to clean water, environmental protection, and sudden social changes. Peru is arguably the country with the greatest challenge in this regard for mine operations and development. However, recently the Chilean government has drafted a legal framework around the ILO-convention 169, which gives certain rights to indigenous populations regarding the use of their land. The proposed framework bears some similarities to that already in place in Peru, and could potentially bring some of the same problems seen in Peru to Chile. This was discussed in detail in our May issue of Copper Studies, which also highlighted recent incidences of community activity.
